Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Let $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ be a basis of $V$, with dual basis
$e^1,\ldots,e^n$. Then the wedges

$$ e^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e^{i_k}\qquad (1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n) $$

form a basis of $\operatorname{Alt}^k(V)$.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

The real **de Rham cohomology** is $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^k(M)/B^k(M)$, with $Z^k,B^k$ as in [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]].

This is [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]] in real vector spaces. Only a closed form $\omega$ represents a class $[\omega]$. For closed forms $\omega,\omega\prime$, equality $[\omega]=[\omega\prime]$ means precisely $\omega\prime-\omega=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$. Addition and real scalar multiplication are induced by those of forms. All groups on the empty manifold are zero.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

derivations.claim: For each increasing $I$, set $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$. By [F3], the $e^I$ form a basis, so this prescription extends uniquely by linearity to a map $\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$; its coefficients are constant, so it also defines a smooth map on the affine space.

For increasing $I,J$ of size $k$, $e^I\wedge e^{J^c}=0$ when $I\ne J$, because an index repeats. When $I=J$, $e^I\wedge\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$. The component pairing has $\langle e^I,e^J\rangle_\eta=0$ for $I\ne J$ and $\langle e^I,e^I\rangle_\eta=\epsilon_I$. Thus the characterizing identity holds on basis pairs and, by bilinearity, for every $\alpha,\beta$. Pairing with all complementary basis wedges also proves uniqueness.

The cycle integral in the Definition is a finite sum of the unique simplex integrals in [F7], so it is independent of how a finite chain is written after equal simplex coefficients are combined. The terms closed, exact, and $[\omega]=0$ have the quotient meanings in [F4] and [F5]. No physical assumption or choice principle is used.

Let $V=\mathbb R^4$ with ordered coframe $e^0=dx^0,e^1=dx^1,e^2=dx^2,e^3=dx^3$, bilinear form $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, inverse $\eta^{-1}=\eta$, and volume form $\mathrm{vol}_\eta=e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. For $0\le k\le4$, give $\Lambda^kV^*$ the induced bilinear pairing $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}$, with indices raised by $\eta^{-1}$. The Lorentzian Hodge star is the unique linear map $\star_\eta:\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$ satisfying $\alpha\wedge\star_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV^*$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The equivalent basis formula is $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$.

For a smooth manifold $N$, an integer $1\le k\le\dim N$, a smooth closed $k$-form $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$, and a finite real smooth singular $k$-cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ with $\partial z=0$, define its period by $\operatorname{Per}_z(\omega):=\int_z\omega:=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$. The form $\omega$ is exact when $\omega=d\alpha$ for a globally defined smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha\in\Omega^{k-1}(N)$. These are mathematical definitions and use no physical constants.

derivations.claim: For any increasing $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$ of size $k$, apply [F1] twice to obtain $\star_\eta^2e^I=\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)e^I$.

The product $\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}$ is $-1$, since the two complementary index sets contain the unique negative metric sign exactly once. Reversing the blocks $I,I^c$ uses $k(4-k)$ transpositions, so $s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)=(-1)^{k(4-k)}$. Thus the general square formula follows on the basis $e^I$. For $I=\{0,1\}$, the star is $-e^{23}$; for $I=\{2,3\}$, it is $e^{01}$, which gives the two displayed special cases.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

Let $V=\mathbb R^4$ with ordered coframe $e^0=dx^0,e^1=dx^1,e^2=dx^2,e^3=dx^3$, bilinear form $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, inverse $\eta^{-1}=\eta$, and volume form $\mathrm{vol}_\eta=e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. For $0\le k\le4$, give $\Lambda^kV^*$ the induced bilinear pairing $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}$, with indices raised by $\eta^{-1}$. The Lorentzian Hodge star is the unique linear map $\star_\eta:\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$ satisfying $\alpha\wedge\star_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV^*$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The form $\omega$ is exact when $\omega=d\alpha$ for a globally defined smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha\in\Omega^{k-1}(N)$. These are mathematical definitions and use no physical constants.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

Let $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:\|p\|_2=1\}$ have its standard embedded smooth structure and outward orientation, let $X(p)=p$, and let $\omega$ be its outward area form, $\omega_p(v,w)=p\cdot(v\times w)$ for tangent vectors $v,w\in T_pS^2$. Put $D=[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$ and
$$

$$
The map $\Phi$ presents $S^2$ as a regular parametrized surface patch, with boundary seam and poles allowed by the patch convention. The outward flux of $X$ is
$$
\int_D (X\circ\Phi)\cdot(\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\phi)\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi.
$$
Equivalently, the oriented top-form integral is $\int_{S^2}\omega=4\pi$.

using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. $$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so

   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,

inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
